title: Epistle to Diognetus
subtitle: every foreign land a homeland: an unknown Christian answers a pagan's questions
lead: The Epistle to Diognetus is a short defense of the Christian faith, written by an unknown Christian to 'most excellent Diognetus', a man of rank who had asked what God the Christians worship, why they despise death, why they reject both the Greek gods and the Jewish observances, what their love for one another is, and why this 'new race' appeared only now (1:1). The writer mocks idols (2), dismisses Jewish sacrifices and customs (3-4), paints Christians as citizens of heaven living everywhere as resident aliens and as the soul of the world (5-6), and tells how God sent not an angel but his own Word, the Creator of all, in gentleness (7-8), why he waited so long, and how the Son became 'a ransom' in 'the sweet exchange' (9). It ends with an appeal to know God and imitate his kindness (10).

Chapters 11-12, which follow in the one manuscript, are another work: Lake calls them 'probably an Epiphany homily', perhaps by Hippolytus, on the Word and the two trees of paradise. The whole text survives in a single manuscript, burned at Strasburg in 1870, and has two gaps (after 7:6 and 10:1). No church counts it as Scripture. Lake says it was probably later than the other Apostolic Fathers and is placed with them by 'custom rather than right'.
facts: No church. It is not among the New Testament books listed by the Council of Trent, the Westminster Confession, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church or Article VI of the Church of England. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it (2240) on the duties of citizens.

Unknown. The lost manuscript seems to have credited it to Justin Martyr; Lake calls the impression the work makes 'quite decisive against' that. Others have proposed Aristides (Lake). The English of the Ante-Nicene Fathers titles it 'The Epistle of Mathetes to Diognetus', from the Greek word for 'disciple' in 11:1. Chapters 11-12: perhaps Hippolytus (Bonwetsch, as Lake reports).

Uncertain. Lake: 'probably later than any of the other writings' among the Apostolic Fathers; Harnack thought the third century more likely than the second; 'there is nothing in the internal evidence to justify any certainty'. The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'anywhere between the Apostles and the age of Constantine'.
No place is named. The writer speaks of Greek and foreign cities, of Jews and Greeks, and of Christians thrown to wild beasts (5:4, 17; 7:7).
An apology (a reasoned defense of the faith) in the form of a letter, in polished rhetorical Greek; then a fragment of a homily (11-12).
Greek. One manuscript of the 1200s or 1300s, once owned by Reuchlin, burned at Strasburg in 1870; three copies made from it in the 1500s; collations made for Otto's editions (Lake's introduction).

12 chapters, 100 verses (no greeting): the letter 1:1-10:8 and the homily 11:1-12:9. The Plain English Translation follows Lake's text throughout, with variant entries for the two gaps, the words supplied at 7:7, and the places where Lake prints an editor's correction of the manuscript.
authorship: The writer gives no name. He writes as a Christian to an outsider, never names Jesus, and quotes no Scripture by formula.

Lake: the general impression the document makes is 'quite decisive against the tradition which seems to have been preserved in the lost MS. ... attributing it to Justin Martyr'. The Catholic Encyclopedia judges Justin 'quite incapable' of its style.

Lake: the letter resembles the Apology of Aristides, and 'the suggestion has been made that it may have been written by Aristides'. The Catholic Encyclopedia lists further proposals, among them Clement of Rome, Apelles and Marcion.

The Ante-Nicene Fathers' English titles it 'The Epistle of Mathetes to Diognetus'. Mathētēs is Greek for 'disciple', the word in 11:1 ('I became a disciple of apostles'), which belongs to the separate homily.
A different document. Lake: 'Bonwetsch has shown very strong reasons for thinking that Hippolytus was the author' (1902).

audience.to: Diognetus, addressed as 'most excellent' (1:1), a man of rank who had asked clear and careful questions about the Christians; who he was is unknown (Lake), and his identification with a teacher of Marcus Aurelius is 'at most plausible' (Catholic Encyclopedia). Through him, educated pagans curious about or hostile to the Christians. Chapters 11-12 were first for a Christian congregation hearing a sermon at a feast.
audience.why: To answer the questions and objections of an outsider: why not the Greek gods, why not the Jewish worship, how Christians live, who their God is, and why the faith came so late, and to invite him to faith and the imitation of God (10). Knowing the audience explains the letter's shape: it argues from reason and from the Christians' lives, mocks idols with Greek wit, quotes the New Testament only by allusion, and speaks of 'the Word', 'the Son' and 'the servant' rather than Jesus' name.
views: A letter to a real inquirer
As the address says: an apology sent to a pagan of rank.
Lake: 'it may be doubted whether it was not an academic treatise or possibly the exercise of some young theologian rather than an actual apology sent to a living person'.

outline: Christians in the world: citizens and strangers
No one knew God; the plan kept and revealed
Why so late; the sweet exchange
Faith and knowledge of the Father ... (gap)
Love God and imitate him (the letter ends)
A separate homily: the Word from the beginning
The two trees of paradise; doxology

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the work as a document of uncertain date and author: the one burned manuscript and its gaps, the failed attribution to Justin, the unknown Diognetus (and the guess at Marcus Aurelius's teacher), whether it was sent to anyone (Lake's doubt), and chapters 11-12 as a separate homily, perhaps by Hippolytus.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the letter's use of Paul, John and 1 Peter, which Lake's margin marks: 'resident aliens', 'citizens of heaven', the paradoxes of 2 Corinthians 6, the Word of John 1, the ransom and the exchange of 2 Corinthians 5:21 and 1 Peter 3:18, and the homily's one formal quotation, 1 Corinthians 8:1.

lenses.name: Apologetics and the Greek world
lenses.desc: Reads it beside the other early defenses of the faith (Aristides, Justin) and the Greek world they addressed: the case against idols, the mockery of philosophers who made God fire or water, Christians as model citizens, and the Logos offered to a pagan reader.

sections.b: The Plain English Translation is made from Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1913), which rests on the one manuscript as collated for Otto's editions. It follows Lake's text throughout. Lake prints no apparatus for Diognetus, and in a dozen places his Greek follows an editor's correction where the manuscript, as Otto's edition of 1879 reports it, reads otherwise (5:7; 7:2; 8:11; 9:1 twice; 9:2; 10:8; 11:1; 11:2; 11:5; 12:8; 12:9): each has a variant entry giving both readings. The two gaps are marked '...' (7:6; 10:1), and at 7:7 the words Lake suggests are supplied in brackets; each has a variant entry. Key words follow the site's other early Christian writings: theosebeia 'reverence for God', deisidaimonia 'superstition', paroikoi 'resident aliens', politeuomai 'live as citizens', pais of the Son 'Child' (8:9, with a note on 'servant'; hypēretēs at 7:2 is 'attendant'), epieikeia 'forbearance' (7:4), logos 'the Word', kolasis 'punishment'. The writer's scorn for Jewish practice (3-4) is translated as it stands.

Lake: 'the unique MS. of the epistle in the library at Strasburg was twice collated for Otto's edition but was destroyed by fire in 1870. This MS., probably written in the thirteenth or fourteenth century, was formerly the property of Reuchlin, passed about 1560 to the Alsatian monastery of Maursmunster, and between 1793 and 1795 came to Strasburg.' It was collated by Cunitz and later by Reuss for Otto. Copies were made by Stephanus in 1586 (Leiden), by Beurer about 1590 (known from Stephanus's collation of 1592) and by Hausius about 1580 (Tübingen), and O. von Gebhardt (1878) gave 'the proof that none of them are more than copies of the Strasburg MS.' So the entire text depends on one lost copy and on the records made of it.

sections.h: Two gaps, and an ending lost
sections.b: The manuscript breaks off twice. After 7:6, Lake: 'There is here a lacuna in the MS.'; he suggests the next sentence began 'Do you not see that'. After 10:1: 'Here again there is apparently a lacuna in the text.' The letter itself stops at 10:8; the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that 'it may have originally been much longer'. Lake marks no gap there.

No one in the early church mentions it (Lake: 'early tradition does not mention the epistle'). Lake judges it 'probably later than any of the other writings' in the Apostolic Fathers and nearer, by its contents, to the works of the Apologists, reports that Harnack thought the third century more likely, and concludes that 'there is nothing in the internal evidence to justify any certainty of opinion'. The Catholic Encyclopedia gives the range as 'anywhere between the Apostles and the age of Constantine', with Harnack's 170-300 and Zahn's 250-310 among the proposals.

sections.h: Two pieces: the letter and the homily
sections.b: Chapters 1-10 are a letter to an outsider; chapters 11-12 are a sermon to believers, with a different style and subject. Lake: they 'have clearly no connection with the preceding ones', 'probably an Epiphany homily, though possibly, as Otto thought, an Easter homily', and Bonwetsch argued for Hippolytus. The site keeps Lake's chapter numbers but treats the two throughout as separate works: the chapter pages, the lenses and the outline mark the break.

Lake: 'Like most early apologies for Christianity it begins by expounding the foolishness of the worship of idols, and the inadequacy of the Jewish religion and then proceeds to give a short sketch of Christian belief, a panegyric on Christian character and a description of the benefit which it offers to converts. In this respect it resembles the apology of Aristides, and somewhat less closely those of Justin and Tatian.' The topic page Defending the Faith follows the practice from 1 Peter 3:15 and Paul's speeches in Acts to these writers.

The letter's lasting gift to Christian thought is chapters 5-6: Christians live in every land 'as resident aliens', 'citizens of heaven' who obey the laws and outdo them, the soul of the world. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes 5:5, 5:10 and 6:10 in its teaching on the duties of citizens (2240). The topic page Strangers and Exiles traces the idea from Abraham to 1 Peter and the early church.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the questions answered in turn
spec.body: This is Claude's reading of the letter's plan, built on Lake's summary of its contents. The five questions of 1:1 seem to be answered in a new order and then gathered up. 'Why not the Greek gods?' is chapter 2; 'why not the Jewish superstition?' is chapters 3-4; 'what is their love for one another?' and 'how do they look down on the world?' are chapters 5-6 (resident aliens, the soul of the world); 'what God do they trust, and how do they worship him?' is chapters 7-8 (the God who sent his Word, seen by faith); 'why now and not earlier?' is chapter 9. Chapter 10 then turns the questions back on Diognetus: if he wants this faith, he too will love, imitate God and think nothing of death (10:7-8). If the plan is right, the letter may be nearly complete at 10:8, even though it breaks off there. Lake's introduction already lists the contents in this order (the idols, the Jewish religion, a sketch of Christian belief, a panegyric on Christian character, the benefit to converts); matching them to the five questions of 1:1 is Claude's own.

canon.summary: The Epistle to Diognetus is an anonymous defense of the faith, of uncertain date, that survived in one manuscript burned in 1870; its last two chapters are a separate homily. It is in no church's Bible and no early writer mentions it. The Catholic Catechism quotes its picture of Christians as resident aliens.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books does not include it. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it in its teaching on the duties of citizens: Christians 'reside in their own nations, but as resident aliens' (2240, citing 5:5, 5:10 and 6:10).
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books does not name it.
Not Scripture: Article VI receives only the books of the New Testament 'as they are commonly received'; it does not mention Diognetus, and the letter has never been among those books.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as Holy Scripture, and the letter is not among them.

provenance.h: An unknown writer, an unknown date
provenance.b: Lake: 'an anonymous writing of uncertain date', 'probably later than any of the other writings' in the Apostolic Fathers, closer to the Apologists; Harnack placed it more probably in the third century; 'early tradition does not mention the epistle'. The Catholic Encyclopedia: 'anywhere between the Apostles and the age of Constantine'.

One Greek manuscript of the 1200s or 1300s, once Reuchlin's, kept at Strasburg and destroyed by fire in 1870, after it had been collated for Otto's editions; copies made from it in the 1500s, which von Gebhardt (1878) proved were only copies (Lake). In it the letter was followed by a separate homily (11-12), and the manuscript seems to have credited the work to Justin Martyr.

rejected_why.b: A book had to be known and read in the churches to be weighed as Scripture. Lake: 'early tradition does not mention the epistle'. It appears in none of the lists of New Testament books given above, and it was found only in a medieval manuscript that credited it, wrongly, to Justin Martyr.

It names no author, claims no apostle's authority, and is probably later than the New Testament by a century or more (Lake). The phrase 'disciple of apostles' belongs to the separate homily of 11-12, and the Catholic Encyclopedia says it was by 'a misunderstanding of these words' that the work was classed among the Apostolic Fathers at all.

cited_in.b: 1 Peter calls believers 'resident aliens and temporary residents' (1 Peter 2:11); the letter's 'they live in their own homelands, but as resident aliens' develops the same word. The New Testament does not refer to the letter.
Paul's 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven' (Philippians 3:20) stands behind 'they live as citizens of heaven'; Lake's margin gives Philippians 3:18-20.
The paradoxes of 5:11-16 are modeled on Paul's (Lake's margin); 5:13 repeats 'We are poor, yet we make many rich' (2 Corinthians 6:10).
The homily of 11-12 quotes Paul by formula, 'the apostle ... says', in the same words: 'Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.' The quotation runs from Paul to the homily, not the other way.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how a Christian could present the faith to an educated pagan, the letter is valuable and its picture of Christians in the world (5-6) is quoted by the Catechism of the Catholic Church (2240); but its date is so uncertain (second or third century, by the views Lake reports) that it cannot be used as firm evidence for any one generation. As a text it is fragile: everything rests on one manuscript, burned in 1870, with two gaps and an ending that may be lost. It makes few historical claims. Its teaching on God, the Word and the cross agrees closely with the New Testament; its treatment of Jewish worship goes beyond and conflicts with the Bible's own account of the Law.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to Christian faith and life
sections.b: High for what it shows of Christian self-understanding: Christians as resident aliens and citizens of heaven (5), the soul of the world (6), the Son as the Creator sent in gentleness (7), the ransom and 'sweet exchange' (9), the imitation of God in generosity (10). Limited because the date and place are unknown (Lake: 'nothing in the internal evidence to justify any certainty'), and because the portrait of chapter 5 is an idealized one offered to an outsider.

Fragile. One manuscript, probably of the 1200s or 1300s, destroyed in 1870; the text is known from the collations made for Otto and from copies of the 1500s that derive from it (Lake). Gaps after 7:6 and 10:1 (variant entries), a likely lost ending after 10:8 (Catholic Encyclopedia), and a separate homily joined to it (11-12). Hard places such as 2:3 and 12:7 cannot be checked against any other witness.

Few. The letter claims to answer a real Diognetus; Lake doubts it was ever sent. It says Christians are persecuted by Jews and Greeks and thrown to wild beasts (5:17; 7:7), which fits what other sources report of the second and third centuries (the Martyrdom of Polycarp, on this site). The homily's 'disciple of apostles' (11:1) is not a claim by the letter's writer, and, if Bonwetsch is right that Hippolytus wrote it, it means a follower of the apostles' teaching, not a hearer of the apostles.

Matches: the folly of idols (2; Psalm 115; Isaiah 44); God who needs nothing (3:4; Acts 17:25); Christians as resident aliens and citizens of heaven (5:5, 9; 1 Peter 2:11; Philippians 3:20); love of enemies (5:15; 6:6; Matthew 5:44); the Word as Creator, sent as God and as man (7:2-4; John 1:1-14); God's patience and the timing of the gift (9:1-2; Romans 3:25-26; Galatians 4:4); the ransom and the righteous for the unrighteous (9:2; Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 3:18); justification in the Son alone (9:4-5; Romans 5:18-19); imitation of God (10:4; Ephesians 5:1). Goes beyond: the denial that anyone knew God before Christ (8:1, 5; compare Romans 1:20); God 'free from anger' (8:8; compare Romans 1:18); the soul imprisoned in the body (6:7; compare Genesis 1:31; 1 Corinthians 15:42-44); the homily's reading of the two trees (12:2-4). Conflicts: the treatment of Jewish sacrifice as no better than offerings to idols (3:5) and of the food laws, Sabbath and circumcision as human folly (4:1-5) conflicts with the Law's account of these as God's commands (Leviticus 1:1-2; Genesis 17:10-11; Exodus 20:8-11) and with Paul's 'the covenants, and the lawgiving, and the sacred service' among Israel's gifts (Romans 9:4). The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate 4 teaches that 'the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God'; the site's topic on Christian anti-Judaism traces where language like this led.

how_to_read.h: As a letter to an outsider
how_to_read.b: Read it as Diognetus would: a cultured pagan hearing why Christians are different. Notice what the writer leaves out for such a reader (Jesus' name, quotations of Scripture) and what he stresses (reason, the Christians' lives, God's kindness).

how_to_read.h: With Paul, John and 1 Peter open
how_to_read.b: The notes mark each echo. Chapters 5-6 read best beside 1 Peter 2:11, Philippians 3:20 and 2 Corinthians 6:9-10; chapters 7-9 beside John 1, Romans 3 and 5, and 2 Corinthians 5:21.
The writer's scorn for Jewish practice is translated as it stands. Read it beside the Law and Romans 9-11, and with the note at 4:1, which sets out how the chapter is weighed today.
Read the homily on its own terms: a preacher to believers on the Word and the trees of paradise, perhaps at a feast, perhaps by Hippolytus. It does not tell us who wrote the letter.
